top.line: The agent drafts and a person sends, in phases
top.para: Two callers asked how to copy my email setup, so this is the walkthrough. Claude runs as a state machine, one session per role, with messages between agents as vault files and every email a draft a person sends. It goes in phases: accounts, one inbox session, split roles, then interfaces and a conductor.

s0.line: Own accounts, written policies, and nothing sent by agents
s0.para: The agent gets its own Workspace mailbox and its own Claude Team seat, never your inbox. Start with one inbox session and a policy written first, then split into roles that talk through Email-FS lite in a vault. Nothing is sent by an agent, except one named security exception with a hold.

s1.line: The setup is copyable, and nothing is clever
s1.para: Two calls ended with the same question, so the walkthrough gets its own page. The simple version takes an afternoon and the full one a week. It is accounts, a policy, drafts and files, and the discipline of the phases makes it work; you can stop at any phase.

s2.line: Each role session reads state, works, writes, stops
s2.para: Claude is good enough to be a step in a state machine. Each role reads its state from vault files, does one kind of work, writes results back as files and stops. Sessions can be opened by hand or scheduled; start with ones you open, so every run is one you watched.

s3.line: The agent needs its own mailbox, seat and grants
s3.para: Phase 0 gives the agent a Workspace mailbox on a domain you own, never your own inbox, plus a separate Claude Team seat whose OAuth grants live only there. Connectors must first be enabled by an organisation owner. Add a GitHub account on the same identity and share your calendar read-only.

s4.line: One inbox session, a policy first, and you send
s4.para: The inbox agent reads, labels, summarises and writes replies as drafts. Its policy is a table of reach, mandate, gap and barriers, and on a Team plan most barriers are honestly just expectations. Each draft leaves a record line with a body hash, and sends are recorded by a different role.

s5.line: Split roles talk in vault files, not the mailbox
s5.para: Roles such as @inbox, @drafts, @crm, @briefs and @dev each have a short policy; only @inbox reads the mailbox and only @drafts writes Drafts. They exchange files through Email-FS lite with typed blocks. Clone time grows with commits: after three days a vault took seven minutes, so commit once per run.

s6.line: Agents build interfaces; a conductor runs every role once
s6.para: Agents built phone cards and waiting-on boards in an afternoon because the data was already vault files, and each interface got its own policy. The record lets you read what agents did. A conductor runs each role once in fixed order, with twelve-minute time boxes and a security role first and last.

s7.line: Agents never send, except one held security alert
s7.para: The drafts role writes, and the person reads and sends. The one exception lets the security role send one critical email to the person and write a hold file that stops every run until the person releases it. A vault key leaked on day five, so a leaked write key now means a new vault.

s8.line: A checklist from accounts to the never-send rule
s8.para: Buy a Workspace seat, create a Claude Team account, enable then connect the connectors, and share your calendar read-only. Write the policy first, run one session for a week, then split roles that talk through Email-FS lite. Read the footprint monthly, watch clone time, and keep the rule: the agent drafts, you send.

s9.line: The agents add their own accounts, starting with @dev
s9.para: The dev agent shipped nineteen releases in eight days, wrote policies for five future roles, and refuses to fix other agents' files. A briefs-drawn roster shows twelve agents, not five, and corrects the schedule: four runs on weekdays, two at weekends, starting and ending with security.
